A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same statistical causal prompting (SCP) framework. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support comparison; retained material can be matched across reformatting and renumbering.

before.justification: v2 reports original causal-discovery experiments on Auto MPG, DWD climate, Sachs protein, and closed health-screening data, including results in Tables 3–4 and Appendix F.

after.justification: v4 retains these empirical results and adds controlled SCP simulations, confidence-sensitivity analyses, and experiments with multiple LLM combinations.

M1.justification: The four-stage framework, prompting Patterns 0–4, probability thresholds, and acyclic prior-knowledge construction remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–2 are rewritten into equivalent pseudocode. New simulations and LLM substitutions evaluate the existing procedure.

E1.justification: The four datasets, represented domains, and original causal-discovery tasks are retained. Section 4.3 adds controlled health-screening scenarios with deliberately modified statistics for implausible and accepted causal edges. Appendix H reuses DWD rather than introducing another dataset.

E2.justification: The PC, Exact Search, and DirectLiNGAM experiments retain the same unaugmented and Pattern 0 comparison conditions. Appendix H varies LLM components within the proposed framework and compares against the existing no-prior baseline; it introduces no separate competing causal-discovery method.

E3.justification: v4 adds coefficient and bootstrap-probability sweeps using manufactured SCD outputs, a Monte Carlo threshold-classification protocol, and all 25 combinations of five LLMs across Steps 2 and 3 under Pattern 0 on DWD. The original benchmark settings and metrics are retained.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 adds controlled tests of rejection of implausible edges and loss of confidence in accepted edges, plus analysis of contrasting generated explanations. New Appendix D examines yes/no consistency, probability fluctuations, and sensitivity of prior-knowledge decisions to thresholds.

E5.justification: v2 already specifies five probability measurements and 1,000 SCD bootstrap resamples. v4 adds regression uncertainty and significance annotations, standard errors for token probabilities and fitted parameters, and Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis. These additions do not establish increased repetition of the original experiments.

E6.justification: Tables 3–4 and the retained appendix probability tables have unchanged results. New findings include confidence values of 0.0493 and 0.9833 for the Age-to-HbA1c example at coefficients 1.25 and 1.30, a simulated threshold-classification AUC of 0.899, and results for additional LLM combinations in Table 18.

T1.justification: Section 4.3 adds reasoning distinguishing conditional from marginal token-generation probabilities. Appendix D introduces a formal yes/no faithfulness condition, symmetry relationships, and Gaussian assumptions for threshold uncertainty. These are auxiliary analytical additions; the existing causal-model equations, graph definitions, and metric derivations are retained.

C1.justification: The four original contributions remain, but v4 adds reliability and critical-error analysis as an explicit fifth contribution. The abstract and conclusion now make successful and failing scenarios, practical-use qualifications, and domain-expert checks central parts of the paper's contribution.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands interpretation of false negatives, variability in generated explanations, and the limits of token probabilities as confidence. It also discusses imperfect yes/no faithfulness, possible overfitting, specialized-domain risks, and the difficulty of scaling expert review. Proposed remedies are presented as future directions rather than validated fixes.

D1.justification: v4 adds a project-specific public-code statement and repository link, whereas v2 links only to third-party tools. It also documents token-probability extraction, simulation grids and sample counts, and additional model identifiers and stage assignments. The original temperature, repetition count, thresholds, and dataset-processing disclosures remain.

R1.justification: The research context expands substantially to in-context learning, LLM-as-a-judge, instruction tuning, hallucination, memorization, bias, and uncertainty, with additions including Brown et al., Carlini et al., Lin et al., and Zheng et al.'s LLM-as-a-judge work. The original positioning against LLM-guided causal-discovery research is retained.

P1.justification: Retained prose receives widespread copyediting, terminology normalization, and some shortening. The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion accommodate the new analyses, and Section 4.3 and Appendices D and H are inserted. Most earlier exposition and the overall section sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v4 adds simulation diagrams and plots, regression and example-output tables, confidence-sensitivity plots, and the LLM-combination table: Figures 3–6 and 15–17, and Tables 5–8 and 18. Existing material is retypeset, resized, and relocated, with revised captions and condensed pseudocode.

improvement.justification: v2 largely left controlled investigation of SCP sensitivity and confidence stability to future work. v4 supplies success and failure simulations, conditional uncertainty analysis, clearer applicability limits, and a project-code link, substantially strengthening readers' ability to assess reliability and reproduce the work. Inconsistent Pattern 2/3 labels in new captions and assumption-dependent Monte Carlo conclusions limit precision, but do not outweigh these gains.
